papers.what_it_is: The Jupyter Book source for a card-fraud handbook, whose Chapter 3 notebook defines a transaction simulator with three rule-based fraud scenarios.

assertions.value: In the handbook simulator, scenario 1 labels every transaction with amount above 220 as fraud; the add_frauds code sets TX_FRAUD to 1 on that condition, so this part of the label is a known function of the amount.
quotes: Any transaction whose amount is more than 220 is a fraud.
assertions.certainty_reason: The rule is stated in the prose and implemented in the code on the same condition.

assertions.value: In the handbook simulator, scenario 2 draws two terminals per day with a seeded sample and marks all transactions on them as fraud for the following 28 days.
assertions.anchor: SimulatedDataset.ipynb add_frauds (lines 1743 to 1747); scenario text line 1712
quotes: All transactions on these terminals in the next 28 days will be marked as fraudulent.
assertions.certainty_reason: Prose and code agree: sample(n=2) per day and a window ending at day+28.

assertions.value: In the handbook simulator, scenario 3 draws three customers per day and, within a 14-day window, picks one third of their transactions at random, multiplies those amounts by 5 and labels them fraud.
assertions.anchor: SimulatedDataset.ipynb add_frauds (lines 1758 to 1770); scenario text line 1714
quotes: In the next 14 days, 1/3 of their transactions have their amounts multiplied by 5 and marked as fraudulent.
assertions.certainty_reason: The code uses random.sample with k equal to int of one third of the window transactions, as the prose says.

assertions.value: In scenario 3 the choice of which compromised-customer transactions become fraud is a random sample, so two transactions of the same customer in the same window with the same features can carry different labels. Under that rule the Bayes error on observable columns alone is not shown to be zero.
quotes: Every day, a list of 3 customers is drawn at random.
assertions.certainty_reason: This is an inference from the code (random subset selection); the source does not compute a Bayes error.

facts.explanation: Scenario descriptions are supported by the code. Scenario 1: amount>220 sets TX_FRAUD=1 (line 1735). Scenario 2: two terminals per day via sample(n=2), window day to day+28 (lines 1743 to 1747). Scenario 3: three customers per day via sample(n=3), window day to day+14, int(n/3) of their transactions chosen by random.sample, amounts times 5 (lines 1758 to 1770). The windows overlap across days, so a transaction can be drawn more than once. The corollary (Bayes error zero given complete state) is not stated by the source. It holds only if state includes the seeded random draws (random_state=day, random.seed(day)). The scenario 3 label is not a function of the transaction columns, so zero error does not hold for models limited to those columns plus derived features. Suggest rewording the fact to separate the scenario rules (supported) from the zero-error corollary (an inference).
facts.quote: Every day, a list of two terminals is drawn at random.

papers.what_it_is: Code for an arXiv paper plus the bestperf library that estimates the Bayes error of binary classification from calibrated soft labels.

assertions.value: bestperf computes the Bayes error as the mean over samples of min(p, 1-p), where p is the posterior probability of the positive class given as a soft label.
assertions.certainty_reason: One-line implementation; correctness as a Bayes error estimate needs the soft labels to be true posteriors.

assertions.value: bestperf can calibrate soft labels by fitting isotonic regression of hard labels on soft labels; the paper abstract claims this gives a statistically consistent estimator under a weaker assumption than earlier work.
quotes: we show that isotonic calibration can provide a statistically consistent estimator under an assumption weaker than that of the previous work
assertions.certainty_reason: Claim is from the authors abstract; the code only shows isotonic fitting, consistency is not checked here.

assertions.value: The authors state that perfectly calibrated soft labels can still give a substantially inaccurate Bayes error estimate.
quotes: even perfectly calibrated soft labels can result in a substantially inaccurate estimate
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors claim in the abstract; proof lives in the paper, not read here.

assertions.value: bestperf scores a Bayes error estimator on noise-injected labels, using lower bound 0.5*noise and upper bound 0.5*noise + (1-noise)*sota, where sota is a known upper bound on the clean-data Bayes error.
assertions.certainty_reason: Direct code; sota is described in the docstring as a known upper bound.
